title: Disable or Modify Tools: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System Log
shortTitle: Disable or Modify Tools: Disable or Modify Linux Audit Sy...
summary: This sub-technique degrades the Linux Audit system, the kernel-level facility that produces the host's security-relevant record of process, file, network, and login activity. Where the Windows counterpart targets a service and a policy store, here the adversary aims at the audit daemon, its rule definitions, and sometimes the library functions the daemon calls. With root privileges that means stopping or disabling the audit service, editing the rule files that are loaded at boot, or interfering with the audit library so events are suppressed before they reach disk. Because these are configuration and daemon-state changes, the artefacts are a modified audit configuration, a stopped or masked service unit, and an unexpected break in an otherwise steady stream of audit events. Detection is best served by shipping audit records off the host in near real time, watching for changes to the audit service and its rule files, and treating any gap in sequence or timestamp as an incident until proven otherwise.

beginner.definition: Linux has a built-in audit system that records important events, such as programs starting and files being opened. This technique means an attacker turns that system off or changes its rules. They may stop the audit service, edit its rule files, or block it in code. The aim is to stop the computer writing down what they do.
beginner.whyItMatters: On many Linux servers, the audit record is the main evidence available after an intrusion. If it is stopped or trimmed, you cannot rebuild the timeline or prove what changed. Attackers with administrator rights can do this quickly. Keeping a live copy of these records on another server is the only reliable protection.
howItWorks: The attacker gains root, which is full administrator rights on the machine.
They stop the audit service, or set it so it will not start again.
They edit the audit rule files so activities they care about are ignored.
Some attackers change the audit library, so calls fail quietly inside programs.
Rules reload or the service stays down, and no further events are written.
The attacker proceeds while the audit record stays silent.
beginner.example: Think of a building where a guard signs a paper log each time a door opens. Someone with a master key removes the pen and the spare log book. The doors still open for anyone with a key, and the guard still stands there. The building looks normal, but nothing has been written down since the pen disappeared.
takeaways: Forward audit records to another host, because local files can be altered.
Alert on changes to the audit service state and its rule files.
Treat any unexpected break in the audit stream as a security incident.

objectives: Explain how this sub-technique differs from its parent by targeting a kernel-level audit facility.
Describe how audit rules define which Linux events are recorded.
Identify the ways the audit daemon can be stopped, disabled, or bypassed.
Recognise configuration and stream artefacts that reveal audit tampering.
Explain why near real-time log forwarding limits the impact of this technique.
